---
title: "Moving to the new Swiss Stats Explorer functions"
description: "Why BFS 0.8.0 has new functions for the Swiss Stats Explorer, how they are different from bfs_get_sse_data() and bfs_get_sse_metadata(), and how to change your code."
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
```

BFS 0.8.0 has three new functions for the
[Swiss Stats Explorer](https://stats.swiss/) (SSE): `bfs_sse_datasets()`,
`bfs_sse_dimensions()` and `bfs_sse_data()`. They replace the old functions
`bfs_get_sse_metadata()` and `bfs_get_sse_data()`.

**Your code keeps working.** The old functions get only bug fixes. For
example, some labels were wrong when a code has no name in your language:
they are now correct (see the NEWS of BFS 0.8.0). But the old functions are now
**deprecated**: when your code uses them, you get a warning (at most once
every 8 hours) that tells you to use the new functions. Please move your
code to the new functions, with the help of this article.

If a package that you use calls the old functions, you get no warning. Only
the authors of this package see the warning, when they test their package.

To hide the warning, for example in a pipeline that you can't change now:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
options(lifecycle_verbosity = "quiet")
```

In the examples, we use the same data as in the article
[Swiss Stats Explorer](swiss-stats-explorer.html): the vacancy rate (the
share of empty homes, in %) of the cantons of Geneva, Zurich and Bern.

```{r}
library(BFS)
library(dplyr)
```

## Why new functions?

Marius Hodel wrote `bfs_get_sse_metadata()` and `bfs_get_sse_data()` for
BFS 0.7. With them, you could use the Swiss Stats Explorer in R for the
first time. With time, data pipelines showed some limits. We can't fix them
without changing the results of the old functions:

- **Speed.** The old functions download the data as XML (SDMX-ML), the
  biggest format of the API, and read it in R. For the same query, the
  CSV format (SDMX-CSV) is about 10 times smaller and much faster to read.
- **Data that is not filtered.** If a name in `query` is not a dimension of
  the dataset (for example, a typo), the old functions ignore it. The data
  is not filtered on this dimension, and nothing tells you.
- **Versions.** A dataset can have several versions, and a new version can
  change the dimensions. The old functions always use the latest version.
  So your pipeline can break when the BFS publishes a new version.
- **Labels.** The names of the dimensions come from the codelists. They are
  sometimes technical (for example "Code list for the 'Statistical
  operation' concept") or not translated.
- **Missing information.** The old functions remove the attributes of each
  value, for example its status (provisional or not).

If we changed the old functions, the results of your pipelines would
change. So the old functions stay the same, and the improvements are in new
functions with new names.

The Swiss Stats Explorer uses a standard SDMX server, the
[.Stat Suite](https://sis-cc.gitlab.io/dotstatsuite-documentation/). The new
functions are a thin layer over its API. They only use what the SDMX
standard defines, and let the server do as much work as possible: it
creates the CSV, gives the labels in your language, finds the latest
version and checks the codes. This means less code in R, and less code
that can break when the API changes.

## The functions side by side

| Old | New | What changes |
|---|---|---|
| (none) | `bfs_sse_datasets()` | New: lists the datasets, with all their versions and their descriptions. |
| `bfs_get_sse_metadata(number_bfs)` | `bfs_sse_dimensions(dataset)` | New column names, better dimension names. |
| `bfs_get_sse_data(number_bfs, query)` | `bfs_sse_data(dataset, filters)` | Faster, checks the filters, same column names in all languages, attributes. |

The arguments:

| `bfs_get_sse_data()` | `bfs_sse_data()` |
|---|---|
| `number_bfs` | `dataset` |
| `query` | `filters` (checked, see below) |
| `start_period`, `end_period` | `start_period`, `end_period` |
| (none) | `first_n`, `last_n`, e.g. `last_n = 1` for the latest value |
| `language` | `language` |
| `variable_value_type = "text"` / `"code"` | `labels = "label"` / `"code"`, or `"both"` (default) |
| `column_name_type = "code"` / `"text"` | (always the dimension ids) |
| `clean_names` | (use `janitor::clean_names()` if you need it) |
| (always the latest version) | `version` |
| (no attributes) | `attributes = TRUE` |

The columns of `bfs_get_sse_metadata()` and `bfs_sse_dimensions()`:

| `bfs_get_sse_metadata()` | `bfs_sse_dimensions()` |
|---|---|
| `code` | `dimension` |
| `text` | `dimension_label` |
| `value` | `value` |
| `valueText` | `value_label` |
| `position_dimension` | `position` |
| (none) | `parent`: the value above, e.g. the canton of a district |

The first five columns are in the same order, so code that selects them by
position keeps working.

## The same query, before and after

Our filters: the vacancy rate of the cantons of Geneva, Zurich and Bern.

```{r}
filters <- list(
  GR_KT_GDE = c("GE", "ZH", "BE"), # the three cantons
  WOHN_ANZAHL = "_T",              # all numbers of rooms
  LEERWOHN_TYP = "_T",             # all types of vacant dwellings
  MEASURE_DIMENSION = "RATE"       # the vacancy rate, in %
)
```

Before, with the old function. You get the deprecation warning:

```{r, warning = TRUE}
old <- bfs_get_sse_data(
  number_bfs = "DF_LWZ_1",
  query = filters,
  start_period = "2020",
  language = "en"
)
old
```

After, with the new function. `labels = "label"` gives the names only, as
`bfs_get_sse_data()` does by default:

```{r}
new <- bfs_sse_data(
  "DF_LWZ_1",
  filters = filters,
  start_period = "2020",
  labels = "label",
  language = "en"
)
new
```

The values are the same. Only the order of the columns is different:
`TIME_PERIOD` now comes after the dimensions.

```{r}
all.equal(
  arrange(old, across(everything())),
  arrange(select(new, all_of(names(old))), across(everything()))
)
```

## What is different

### A typo in the filters is an error

With `bfs_get_sse_data()`, a dimension with a typo is ignored. This query
has a typo in `MEASURE_DIMENSION`. So it returns both measures (the number
of vacant dwellings and the rate), not only the rate:

```{r}
typo <- list(GR_KT_GDE = "GE", WOHN_ANZAHL = "_T", LEERWOHN_TYP = "_T",
             MEASURE_DIMENSON = "RATE")

old_typo <- bfs_get_sse_data("DF_LWZ_1", query = typo, start_period = "2020")
n_distinct(old_typo$MEASURE_DIMENSION)
```

`bfs_sse_data()` stops with an error:

```{r, error = TRUE}
bfs_sse_data("DF_LWZ_1", filters = typo, start_period = "2020")
```

You also get an error for `TIME_PERIOD` in `filters`, for filters without a
name, for a dimension given twice, and for an empty vector of codes or
`NA`. The API checks the codes: a code that is not in the dataset gives no
data.

### You can choose the version

`bfs_sse_datasets()` lists all the versions of each dataset:

```{r}
bfs_sse_datasets() |>
  filter(dataset == "DF_LWZ_1")
```

By default, the API uses the latest version. In a pipeline, set `version`
to keep the same structure until you update your code:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
bfs_sse_data("DF_LWZ_1", filters = filters, version = "1.1.0")
```

### The column names are the same in all languages

`bfs_sse_data()` always uses the dimension ids as column names, for example
`GR_KT_GDE`, in all languages. So your code does not break if you change
the language, or if a label changes. By default (`labels = "both"`), you
get the codes, and the labels in a new `<dimension>_label` column:

```{r}
bfs_sse_data(
  "DF_LWZ_1",
  filters = filters,
  start_period = "2026",
  language = "fr"
)
```

Why both by default? Two codes can have the same label. For example, in
`DF_LWZ_1`, the canton of Zurich (`ZH`) and the city of Zurich (`261`) are
both "Zürich". With the labels only, you can't tell their rows apart.

If you used `column_name_type = "text"`, rename the columns with the labels
of `bfs_sse_dimensions()`:

```{r}
dims <- bfs_sse_dimensions("DF_LWZ_1", language = "en") |>
  distinct(dimension, dimension_label)

new |>
  rename_with(~ dims$dimension_label[match(.x, dims$dimension)], all_of(dims$dimension))
```

### Better names for the dimensions

`bfs_get_sse_metadata()` uses the name of the codelist of each dimension.
`bfs_sse_dimensions()` uses the name of its concept. This is the name you
see on stats.swiss:

```{r}
old_labels <- bfs_get_sse_metadata("DF_LWZ_1", language = "en") |>
  distinct(code, old_label = text)
new_labels <- bfs_sse_dimensions("DF_LWZ_1", language = "en") |>
  distinct(dimension, new_label = dimension_label)

left_join(old_labels, new_labels, by = c("code" = "dimension"))
```

The names of the values do not change.

### You can keep the attributes

With `attributes = TRUE`, `bfs_sse_data()` adds the attributes of each
value after `value`, with their labels as for the dimensions. For example,
`OBS_STATUS` is the status of the value (provisional, estimated, ...). The
attributes can change from one version of a dataset to another:

```{r}
bfs_sse_data(
  "DF_LWZ_1",
  filters = filters,
  start_period = "2026",
  attributes = TRUE,
  language = "en"
)
```

### Each error has a class

| Situation | `bfs_get_sse_data()` | `bfs_sse_data()` |
|---|---|---|
| No data for the query | error without a class: "No records found" for most datasets, "HTTP error: 404" for some | error `bfs_no_records` |
| Unknown dimension in the filters | ignored | error `bfs_sse_filter_error` |
| Old argument name, e.g. `query` | (not possible) | error `bfs_sse_argument_error` |
| Unknown dataset or version | error | error `bfs_sse_dataset_error` |
| Query refused by the API, e.g. a wrong period | error without a class: "HTTP error", with the message of the API | error `bfs_sse_query_error`, with the message of the API |
| API not available | error `bfs_http_error` | error `bfs_http_error` |

Handle them in a pipeline with `tryCatch()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
tryCatch(
  bfs_sse_data("DF_LWZ_1", filters = filters),
  bfs_no_records = function(e) NULL
)
```

### It is faster

For small queries, both functions take about one second. The new function
first gets the dimensions of the dataset (a few kilobytes), then the data.
The bigger the data, the bigger the difference: in our tests, for a dataset
of 344,000 values, `bfs_sse_data()` took 6 seconds and
`bfs_get_sse_data()` 28 seconds, with 6 times more memory.

## How to change your code

If you only change the name of the function, and keep the old arguments,
you get an error. It tells you the new name of each argument:

```{r, error = TRUE}
bfs_sse_data(number_bfs = "DF_LWZ_1", query = filters)
```

After `dataset`, you must write the name of each argument. For example,
`bfs_sse_data("DF_LWZ_1", "en")` is an error: write
`bfs_sse_data("DF_LWZ_1", language = "en")`.

The steps:

1. Replace `bfs_get_sse_metadata()` with `bfs_sse_dimensions()`. Rename the
   columns you use (see the table above).
2. Replace `bfs_get_sse_data(number_bfs = ..., query = ...)` with
   `bfs_sse_data(dataset = ..., filters = ...)`. Replace
   `variable_value_type` with `labels`. If you used the default
   (`variable_value_type = "text"`), use `labels = "label"`.
3. Remove `column_name_type` and `clean_names`. If your code uses the
   labels as column names, rename the columns as shown above.
4. If your code selects columns by their position: `TIME_PERIOD` now comes
   after the dimensions. It is safer to select columns by their name.
5. Set `version` to the version you use today (see `bfs_sse_datasets()`).
6. Compare the old and the new results once, as in
   [the same query, before and after](#the-same-query-before-and-after).
   Then switch.
